condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal

claims.claim: Mannitol, a small polar hexitol, has absolute oral bioavailability of 63% in healthy adult men and ~20-24% in colonoscopy patients at 50-150 g doses; L2 adds ~20% and ~0.5 fraction-absorbed records, supporting F>=20% for polar small molecules.

Sorbitol, another hexitol, shows F=0.36-0.38 in shunted patients and 0.27-0.29 in cirrhotic patients; the zero values in normal volunteers are attributed to complete hepatic first-pass removal, not poor absorption, and are not transferable to ascorbic acid.

Glucose, a polar monosaccharide, shows F=0.722-0.843 in healthy/T1DM humans, 38% in children, and 70-100% in OGTT estimates; L2 adds high values in birds and ponies, supporting high F for actively absorbed polar sugars.
Propylene glycol, a small polar diol, has very high/close-to-complete oral bioavailability, supporting that small polar molecules can exceed 20%.
Gemcitabine's low oral bioavailability (10%, poor) is attributed to first-pass metabolism by cytidine deaminase; ascorbic acid lacks this liability, so this low-F context is not transferable.
Additional contexts (topiramate >80%, frusemide ~40%, gallium maltolate 25-57%, pipemidic acid 93%, diflunisal 89.5%) support F>=20% but have lower structural transferability.

The physicochemical prior's unfavorable passive permeability is uncertain; its own caveat notes active transport (SVCT1/2) could significantly enhance ascorbic acid absorption, and the empirical pattern of high F in polar small molecules supports F>=20%.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for ascorbic acid is present in the supplied cards; all support is transfer-based.
Ascorbic acid absorption is dose-dependent via SVCT1/2; the threshold F>=20% may not hold at very high gram doses, but typical oral doses are not specified.
Sorbitol zero-F normal records show first-pass can dominate for polyols; relevance to ascorbic acid is uncertain without direct hepatic extraction data.
Some context cards have canonical SMILES mismatching the named drugs (frusemide, pipemidic acid, diflunisal), reducing transferability.
No formulation, dose, or species match for ascorbic acid is provided.
